claims.claim: The work “To Vigilius on Jewish Unbelief” is a Latin letter written by an otherwise unknown Christian author who identifies himself as Cels (sometimes called Celsus Africanus).
The letter is addressed to a bishop named Vigilius, who is identified in the text as “Vigilius episcopus”.
Cels wrote the letter as a cover note to his Latin translation of the lost Greek dialogue “Jason and Papiscus”, asking Vigilius to correct the translation.
The letter’s purpose is to argue against Jewish “unbelief”, presenting an anti‑Jewish polemic that reflects the hostile Christian‑Jewish relations of its time.
The text survives only in medieval manuscripts that transmit the spurious Cyprianic corpus; the earliest witnesses are two ninth‑century manuscripts (e.g., Reg. Lat. 118, fol. 17‑177v).

In those manuscripts the letter is transmitted under the heading “Ad Vigilium episcopum de iudaica incredulitate” and has been traditionally ascribed to St. Cyprian, which is why modern editions list it among the works of Pseudo‑Cyprian.

Scholars consider the letter valuable because it preserves fragments of the otherwise lost “Dialogue of Jason and Papiscus” and shows how early Christians used such dialogues to promote anti‑Jewish arguments.
